passages.happening:
Manasseh is twelve when he becomes king, and he reigns fifty-five years in Jerusalem (verse 1). He does evil, following the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out (verse 2). He rebuilds the high places his father Hezekiah had destroyed, raises altars for Baal, makes an Asherah pole as Ahab had done, and worships all the host of heaven (verse 3). He builds altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, “In Jerusalem I will put My Name” (verse 4), and in both its courtyards he builds altars to the host of heaven (verse 5).

‘He sacrificed his own son in the fire, practiced sorcery and divination, and consulted mediums and spiritists’ (verse 6). He sets up the carved Asherah pole in the temple itself, the house where the LORD had promised to establish his Name forever (verse 7). ‘But the people did not listen and Manasseh led them astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 18 to 20 showed Judah at its best under Hezekiah. This chapter shows how quickly it could be lost. Manasseh is the Ahab of Judah, and the narrator makes the comparison himself. For Kings his reign is the point of no return: from here on the fall of Jerusalem is announced as certain, and even Josiah's great reform will not reverse it.

Manasseh reigned about 697 to 642 BC, probably at first beside his father. His fifty-five years are the longest reign of any king of Israel or Judah. These were the decades when Assyria was at the height of its power under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, and Assyrian inscriptions name Manasseh of Judah among the western kings who sent tribute and building materials. Judah survived as a loyal vassal. Some scholars think his religious policy reflects that world, especially the worship of the heavenly bodies prominent in Mesopotamia; others note that most of these practices were old Canaanite ones.

Almost every item in the list is forbidden by name in Deuteronomy. The host of heaven means the sun, moon and stars worshiped as gods. Sorcery, divination, mediums and spiritists were ways of seeking hidden knowledge from spirits or the dead. The Asherah pole was an image of the goddess Asherah, and setting it up in the house where the LORD had placed his Name was the worst profanation. Each sin reverses something from Judah's past: what Hezekiah destroyed, Manasseh rebuilt. The narrator quotes the LORD's own promises about the temple against the king who defiled it.

The text names the sacrifice of his son as one item in the list and does not describe it, and these notes do the same.
passages.later: The law forbade anyone who ‘casts spells, consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead’ (Deuteronomy 18:11). Jeremiah later spoke of judgment ‘because of what Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah did in Jerusalem’ (Jeremiah 15:4).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take the sacrifice of a child by a king of David's line?

The text names it plainly among Manasseh's abominations and does not dwell on it. With his grandfather Ahaz, he is one of two kings of Judah of whom it is said. The prophets call such sacrifice the shedding of innocent blood, and Kings counts it among the reasons the city fell. Nothing in the chapter softens it, and nothing in these notes will.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Manasseh undid in a few years what his father had built. Ask what practices in your life or your community protect what earlier faithfulness built. And ask how those in authority over others shape their faith, for good or ill.

passages.t: A bowl wiped and turned upside down
passages.happening:
The LORD speaks through his servants the prophets. Because Manasseh has done these abominations, more wicked than the Amorites before him, the LORD will bring such disaster on Jerusalem and Judah that the ears of all who hear of it will ring (verses 10-12). ‘I will stretch out over Jerusalem the measuring line used against Samaria and the plumb line used against the house of Ahab, and I will wipe out Jerusalem as one wipes out a bowl’ (verse 13). The LORD will forsake the remnant of his inheritance and give them to their enemies, ‘because they have done evil in My sight and have provoked Me to anger from the day their fathers came out of Egypt until this day’ (verse 15).

‘Moreover, Manasseh shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem from end to end’ (verse 16). He dies and is buried in his palace garden, the garden of Uzza, and his son Amon reigns (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The images of judgment come from building and household life. A measuring line, qav, and a plumb line were used to check that a wall was straight. The LORD will measure Jerusalem by the same standard he used for Samaria and for Ahab's house, with the same result. Being the chosen city did not exempt Jerusalem; it made its sins weigh more. Wiping a bowl and turning it upside down leaves nothing in it. The verb, machah, is the one used when Israel's name was not yet to be blotted out, and in the flood story.

Innocent blood, naqi, is the life of someone who did nothing to deserve death. The law treated its shedding as a stain on the land that had to be answered. Verse 16 adds bloodshed to idolatry as a separate charge: false worship and violence against the vulnerable go together.

Burial in a palace garden rather than the royal tombs may have been a mark of dishonor, though the reason is not given.
passages.later: Isaiah had said, ‘I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level’ (Isaiah 28:17). Chronicles adds that Manasseh, taken captive, ‘sought the favor of the LORD his God and earnestly humbled himself’ (2 Chronicles 33:12), and that ‘Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God’ (2 Chronicles 33:13).
passages.hard:
If Manasseh repented, as Chronicles says, why does Kings still blame him for Jerusalem's fall? And why should later generations suffer for his sins?

Kings never mentions Manasseh's repentance. Chronicles, written later and with different emphases, reports that he was taken captive, humbled himself and was restored, and that he removed foreign gods from the temple. Some historians think Chronicles keeps a real episode that Kings left out because it did not change the outcome. Others think the Chronicler shaped the story to teach a theme dear to him, that God answers repentance in every generation. Readers who accept both accounts often note that Manasseh's own repentance came late and did not undo decades of leadership, as Amon's reign shows.

Kings does not claim that innocent people were punished for someone else's guilt. It says that the people followed him and had provoked the LORD from the exodus until that day. Manasseh's reign is the decisive example of a long pattern, not the whole cause. Jeremiah and Ezekiel, preaching before the fall, insisted that each generation was answerable for its own sins. This chapter gives no one a right to blame a whole people for what one ruler did, or to punish children for their parents.
passages.asks: The LORD said he would measure Jerusalem with the same line as Samaria. Ask where you think your privileges excuse you from the standards you apply to others. And ask what innocent blood, in your own time and place, you have learned to walk past.

passages.happening: Amon is twenty-two when he becomes king, and he reigns two years in Jerusalem (verse 19). He does evil as his father did, serves his father's idols and abandons the LORD, the God of his fathers (verses 20-22). His servants conspire against him and kill him in his palace (verse 23). ‘But the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against King Amon, and they made his son Josiah king in his place’ (verse 24). Amon is buried in the garden of Uzza (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Amon reigned about 642 to 640 BC. His short account simply repeats his father's pattern.

The people of the land were probably Judah's landowning citizens. They had acted before to secure the throne for David's line after Athaliah, and they act again here. They make a boy king, and that boy will be Josiah.
passages.later: Matthew's family tree of Jesus runs through these kings: ‘Hezekiah was the father of Manasseh, Manasseh the father of Amon, Amon the father of Josiah’ (Matthew 1:10).
passages.asks: Amon walked in all his father's ways, and his son would walk in none of them. Ask which of your parents' ways you have carried on without choosing them. And ask what it would take to choose differently.
